claims.text: In single-phase disordered BCC high-entropy alloys, increasing atomic-size mismatch increases lattice distortion.
Increased lattice distortion creates localized stress fields that impede or pin dislocations.
Greater dislocation pinning requires higher applied stress for dislocation motion.
Greater dislocation pinning raises yield strength.
Equiatomic TaNbHfZrTi is an example of a single-phase disordered BCC HEA suitable as the initial state.
Substituting constituents with elements of significantly different atomic radius will increase overall atomic-size mismatch.
Alloys with intentionally increased atomic-size mismatch will have higher hardness than the low-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with intentionally increased atomic-size mismatch will have higher yield strength than the low-mismatch baseline.
In situ TEM will show a higher density of pinned or slowed dislocations in the increased-mismatch alloys.
A BCC HEA whose constituents have minimal atomic-size differences will have relatively low lattice distortion.

The proposed size-mismatch strengthening relationship should hold from room temperature to about 600 degrees Celsius at conventional strain rates, provided the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution.
If phase separation or high-temperature instability occurs, mechanisms other than lattice-distortion-mediated dislocation pinning may dominate.
Emerging short-range order may influence dislocation behavior independently of atomic-size mismatch.
XRD lattice-parameter measurements can quantify the relevant lattice distortion.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength, or failure to observe increased dislocation pinning, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
